# OPERATION — jarvis_os

This project is managed by **Jarvis**, the agentic OS. This file is the operating
contract every agent working here must follow.

## How work arrives

1. Work orders are created via `jarvis wo create jarvis_os "..."`, the Jarvis web
   UI, or (discouraged) direct insert into `.jarvis/jarvis.db`.
2. The Jarvis daemon polls this project's queue (`.jarvis/jarvis.db`, gitignored) and
   spawns one Claude Code background worker per work order, in a fresh git worktree.
3. The worker owns the work order end to end. It may brainstorm, invoke skills, spawn
   subagents, or run workflows — its call. It works autonomously toward a complete
   solution unless the work order says otherwise.

## Worker obligations

While handling work order `$JARVIS_WO_ID`, you MUST:

- **Work in your assigned worktree** (you are started in it). Commit your work; push
  and open a PR following this repo's conventions. Never push to main.
- **Title the PR `[$JARVIS_WO_ID] <what it does>`** — the work order id verbatim, in
  square brackets, first. That prefix is what ties the pull request back to the work
  order for everyone who never sees Jarvis, so `gh pr create` with any other title is
  blocked by the hook.
- **Route any doubt to Neo — it is your first responder**:
  `jarvis wo ask "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<your question>"`, then end your turn.

  The answer arrives as your next user turn, usually within a minute, from Neo (the
  user's delegate) or the user. This is the *normal, expected* way to work: it is not
  an escalation, it does not interrupt the user, and it costs you about a minute. Put
  everything needed to decide inside the question text — whoever answers sees only
  that text, never your session — with the concrete options and your recommendation.

  The trigger is **doubt**, not importance. If you catch yourself weighing options,
  thinking "either would work", or picking one because you have to pick something, you
  are in doubt: ask, *before* you build on it.

  Do not talk yourself out of asking. "It's reversible", "it's only an implementation
  detail", "I'll note it as an assumption" — those are rationalisations for guessing.
  Almost everything is reversible; that is not the question. The question is whether
  you would be *rebuilding* if you guessed wrong.
- **Record the calls you were sure about** — this should be rare:
  `jarvis wo assume "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<the assumption>"`

  An assumption is for the *other* case: a call you made with **no doubt** — you
  followed an existing convention, the work order implied it, the codebase left one
  sensible option. Record every such call, including the small and obvious ones
  (naming, file layout, which convention you followed, how you split the commits):
  recording is cheap and the work order record is the only audit trail anyone gets. It
  appends to ASSUMPTIONS.md and flags the work order for review.

  An assumption is a disclosure of something you were *sure* about. It is never a
  guess you are hoping nobody checks — if you are guessing, ask instead.
- **File deferred work in the central backlog** instead of leaving "future work" notes:
  `jarvis backlog add jarvis_os "<title>" --description "<details>"`
- **Report reusable learnings** (patterns, gotchas, good practices) to the OS knowledge
  base so other projects benefit:
  `jarvis learn add "<what you learned>" --project jarvis_os --topic "<topic>"`
  The knowledge base is the only memory the OS can see. Private memory files are
  mirrored into it when written, but what you say here lands intact.
- **Report bugs in Jarvis OS itself** (a `jarvis` command fails, hangs, or does the
  wrong thing) with your `report-jarvis-bug` skill, then carry on. Bugs in *this*
  project are not Jarvis OS bugs — those go to the backlog.
- **Notify on things needing human attention**:
  `jarvis notify --project jarvis_os --level warning|critical "<title>" "<body>"`
- **Summarize your result** when done:
  `jarvis wo finish "$JARVIS_WO_ID" --summary "<what was delivered, where>"`
  then write your full answer as the last thing you say.

  If you opened a pull request, pass it as well: `--pr <url>`. The work order then
  parks in **waiting for PR merge** — it stays on the user's open list with the link
  until they merge it, instead of settling as completed work nobody is looking at.

## What the outside world sees

The work order record IS this conversation, as far as anyone else is concerned. The last
message of every turn you take is captured verbatim into it, and the user and Neo decide
from that record — neither will ever open your session.

So end every turn with the complete answer: findings, caveats, uncertainties, what you
did NOT do, and absolute paths. `--summary` is a one-line headline for that answer, never
a substitute for it. The same goes for `jarvis wo ask` — put everything needed to decide
inside the question text, because whoever answers sees only that text.

## Interacting with the user

The user may reply through Jarvis or the UI; those messages arrive as new user turns in
your session. Treat them as authoritative feedback on the current work order.

## Privileged actions

These actions are **gated, not forbidden**: you may attempt them, and an
independent reviewer (Neo, the user's delegate) decides whether they run.

- `pr_merge` — merge a pull request into the default branch
- `release` — cut a release and deploy it (this reaches the live production fleet)
- `service_restart` — restart or stop a system service (this interrupts the running fleet)

Ask before acting — the reviewer sees ONLY the text you write, so a request with
evidence is far more likely to be approved than a bare attempt:

```bash
jarvis gate request "$JARVIS_WO_ID" "<the exact command>" \
    --why "<why this is ready to ship>" \
    --evidence "<PR number, test results, checks>"
```

Then END YOUR TURN. The verdict arrives as your next user turn. If approved, run
that exact command — the grant is scoped to that one string and expires, so do
not reword it. If denied, fix what the reason names; retrying unchanged will be
blocked again.

There is a third verdict, **dismissed**. The gate recognises commands by matching
text, so it sometimes fires on one that merely *names* a privileged action — a
release script inside a grep pattern, a path quoted in a PR body. That is a defect
in the OS, not a refusal: the reviewer dismisses it, nothing is authorised, and the
command goes through unchanged. So when a gate fires on something you know ships
nothing, do not reword the command to slip past it. File the request, say plainly
why it performs no privileged action, and end your turn.
